question: Light passes from air into medium A and then into medium B through parallel interfaces. The absolute refractive indices are 1.6 for A and 1.2 for B. The angle of incidence in air is 45^°. Which conclusion is correct if the ray propagates through both interfaces?

options.text: The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the A–B interface because 1.6>1.2.
The ray emerges into B at 45^°, since the first and second interfaces are parallel.
The ray travels at approximately 36.1^° to the normal in B.
The ray travels at approximately 53.1^° to the normal in B.

explanation:
At parallel interfaces, Snell's law gives


1sin45^°=1.2sin r_B



sin r_B=(0.7071 / 1.2)=0.5893


Therefore,


r_B≈36.1^°


The ray can propagate through B because the angle in A is below the critical angle for the A–B interface. The final angle depends on the refractive index of B relative to air, not merely on the fact that the interfaces are parallel.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Can total internal reflection occur at normal incidence?
question: A ray travels from glass into air at normal incidence. The refractive index of glass is 1.5. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs because glass is optically denser than air.
The ray is reflected completely because the angle of incidence is 90^°.
The ray emerges at the critical angle of 41.8^°.
The ray emerges undeviated, although its speed increases as it enters air.

explanation: At normal incidence, the angle of incidence is 0^°, not 90^°. Total internal reflection requires incidence above the critical angle. The ray passes into air without changing direction, and its speed increases from c/1.5 to approximately c.

title: Combining critical angle and speed
question: A transparent material has a critical angle of 30^° when surrounded by air. A ray travels through it at an incidence angle of 35^° at the material–air interface. Which combination is correct?

options.text: The refractive index is 2, the speed is 1.5×10^8 m/s, and total internal reflection occurs.
The refractive index is 0.5, the speed is 6×10^8 m/s, and refraction occurs.
The refractive index is sqrt2, the speed is 2.12×10^8 m/s, and refraction occurs.
The refractive index is 2, the speed is 3×10^8 m/s, and refraction occurs.

explanation:
n=frac1{sin30^°}=2



v=(3×10^8 / 2)=1.5×10^8 m/s


Since 35^°>30^°, total internal reflection occurs. Option D uses the speed in vacuum rather than in the material.

question: A transparent liquid layer of thickness 4 cm and refractive index 1.25 lies above a second liquid layer of thickness 6 cm and refractive index 1.5. A small object is at the bottom. What is its apparent depth from the top surface when viewed normally from air?

d_{apparent}=

title: Refraction, speed and wavelength
question: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters a transparent medium of refractive index 1.5. It then enters a second medium of refractive index 1.2, with both indices measured relative to air. What is the wavelength in the second medium?

options.text: 400 nm
600 nm
720 nm
500 nm

explanation:
The wavelength in the second medium is


lambda₂=frac{lambda_{air}}{n₂}
=(600 / 1.2)=500 nm


**Correction:** The correct answer is **D, 500 nm**. Frequency remains unchanged across both interfaces.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why the emergent ray is parallel
question: A student claims that the emergent ray from a rectangular glass slab is parallel to the incident ray because the ray bends towards the normal at both surfaces. Which correction is most accurate?

options.text: The ray bends towards the normal at the first surface and away from the normal at the second surface; the opposite angular deviations cancel.
The ray bends away from the normal at both surfaces.
The ray does not bend at either surface if the slab is rectangular.
The ray becomes parallel to the incident ray only when total internal reflection occurs at both surfaces.

explanation: The first surface causes bending towards the normal when light enters glass from air. The second causes bending away from the normal when light returns to air. Because the surfaces are parallel, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, although laterally displaced.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Mirage and total internal reflection
question: Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between atmospheric refraction and total internal reflection in a mirage?

options.text: Every mirage is caused exclusively by total internal reflection at a sharp air–air boundary.
A mirage is caused by the atmosphere having a refractive index of exactly zero near the ground.
A mirage occurs because sunlight changes frequency as it passes through hot air.
A mirage arises from a temperature-dependent refractive-index gradient; sufficiently strong bending and total internal reflection can contribute under suitable conditions.

explanation: A mirage is an atmospheric optical phenomenon. Temperature gradients alter the refractive index of air and curve light paths. Total internal reflection can be involved in suitable ray paths, but it is not correct to say that every mirage arises exclusively from reflection at a sharp boundary.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: A ray at the critical angle
question: A glass–air interface has a critical angle of 42^°. A ray inside glass is incident at exactly 42^°. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs, and no refracted ray exists.
The refracted ray travels along the interface, while the incident angle remains 42^°.
The ray refracts into air at an angle of 42^°.
The ray travels normally into air because its incidence angle equals the critical angle.

explanation: At the critical angle, the refracted ray makes 90^° with the normal and therefore travels along the interface. Total internal reflection occurs when the incidence angle exceeds 42^°, not when it equals 42^°.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refractive index from two measured angles
question: A ray travels from medium A into medium B. The incidence angle is 60^°, and the refraction angle is 45^°. What is the refractive index of B relative to A?
explanation:
n_{BA}=(sin60^° / sin45^°)



n_{BA}=(0.8660 / 0.7071)
≈1.225


The index is greater than 1, consistent with the ray bending towards the normal on entering B. Option A gives the reciprocal.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Two different critical angles
question: Media P and Q have absolute refractive indices 1.5 and 1.25. They are each surrounded by air. Which statement is correct?

options.text: P has the smaller critical angle and the lower speed of light.
P has the larger critical angle and the lower speed of light.
Q has the smaller critical angle and the lower speed of light.
Both media have equal critical angles because they are surrounded by air.

explanation:
For P,


C_P=sin^{-1}(1/1.5)≈41.8^°


For Q,


C_Q=sin^{-1}(1/1.25)≈53.1^°


P has the smaller critical angle. Its higher refractive index also means a lower speed of light.

title: Apparent shift with increasing depth
question: A liquid has refractive index 1.5. An object is viewed vertically from air, first at a real depth of 8 cm and then at 16 cm. What happens to the apparent shift?

options.text: It decreases from 2.67 cm to 1.33 cm.
It remains unchanged because the refractive index is constant.
It doubles from approximately 2.67 cm to 5.33 cm.
It quadruples from 2.67 cm to 10.67 cm.

explanation:
Shift=d≤ft(1-frac1nright)


At 8 cm,


8≤ft(1-frac1{1.5}right)
≈2.67 cm


At 16 cm,


16≤ft(1-frac1{1.5}right)
≈5.33 cm


The shift doubles because it is proportional to real depth for a fixed refractive index.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Speed and frequency through successive media
question: A monochromatic source emits light of frequency 5×10^ Hz. The light travels through air, glass of refractive index 1.5, and water of refractive index 4/3. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Frequency is highest in glass and lowest in air.
Frequency remains constant; speed is lowest in glass, and wavelength in water is greater than in glass.
Frequency decreases in each successive medium, while speed remains constant.
Speed is highest in glass because its refractive index is highest.

explanation: Frequency remains unchanged across stationary interfaces. The speeds are c in air, c/1.5 in glass, and c/(4/3) in water. Water's speed is greater than glass's, so its wavelength is also greater at the same frequency.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Total internal reflection at a liquid–air interface
question: A ray travels inside a liquid of refractive index 1.4 and strikes a liquid–air interface at 50^°. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It refracts into air at an angle of 50^°.
It refracts into air at an angle of 90^°.
It undergoes total internal reflection because the critical angle is approximately 45.6^°.
It refracts towards the normal because the liquid is denser than air.

explanation:
C=sin^{-1}≤ft(frac1{1.4}right)
≈45.6^°


Since 50^°>C, total internal reflection occurs. Option B would describe the limiting case at the critical angle, not an angle above it.

title: Refractive index and wavelength in a medium
question: The wavelength of light in air is 480 nm. In a transparent material, the wavelength becomes 320 nm. Assuming the frequency remains unchanged, calculate the refractive index of the material relative to air.
explanation:
Since frequency is unchanged, the refractive index is the ratio of the wavelength in air to the wavelength in the material:


n=frac{lambda_{air}}{lambda_{medium}}
=(480 / 320)=1.5


Option A reverses the wavelength ratio.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Reversing a ray through a prism
question: A ray passes through a transparent prism along a particular path. The direction of the ray is then reversed exactly along its emergent path. Which statement follows from the principle of reversibility of light?

options.text: The ray retraces the original path in reverse, provided the optical conditions remain unchanged.
The ray follows a different path because the prism's refractive index changes with direction.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at every surface during reverse travel.
The ray emerges parallel to its original incident direction regardless of the prism angle.

explanation: The laws of refraction and reflection are reversible. Reversing the direction along an established ray path makes the light retrace that path in reverse. It does not guarantee that the prism's emergent ray is parallel to the original incident ray.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comparing a bubble's apparent depth for two colours
question: An air bubble lies inside glass. When viewed normally from air, its apparent depth is calculated using the refractive index of the glass. Which statement is generally correct for ordinary glass in the visible range?

options.text: Blue light gives a greater apparent depth because its refractive index is higher.
Blue and red light give identical apparent depths because their frequencies are different.
Red light gives a smaller apparent depth because its refractive index is lower.
Red light generally gives a greater apparent depth because its refractive index is lower than that for blue light.

explanation: Apparent depth is d_{real}/n. Ordinary glass generally has a lower refractive index for red light than for blue light. Thus, for the same real depth, red light gives a greater apparent depth.

The critical angle is approximately 41.8^°, so the ray refracts into air.
The critical angle is 48.2^°, so total internal reflection occurs.
The critical angle is 30^°, so the ray undergoes total internal reflection.

A) Total internal reflection occurs because the refractive index is greater than 1.

B) The critical angle is approximately 41.8^°, so the ray refracts into air.

C) The critical angle is 48.2^°, so total internal reflection occurs.

D) The critical angle is 30^°, so the ray undergoes total internal reflection.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:**


C=sin^{-1}(1/1.5)≈41.8^°

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comprehensive concept check
question: Consider the following statements: I. Frequency remains unchanged when light crosses a stationary boundary. II. A parallel-sided slab produces lateral displacement for oblique incidence, even though the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. III. Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium and the incidence angle is smaller than the critical angle. IV. The critical angle decreases as the refractive index of the denser medium increases, provided the rarer medium remains air. Which combination is correct?

options.text: I and II only.
I, II and IV only.
II, III and IV only.
I, II, III and IV.

explanation:
- I is true: frequency remains unchanged at a stationary boundary.
- II is true: parallel slab faces restore the emergent direction but generally leave lateral displacement.
- III is false: total internal reflection requires an incidence angle greater than the critical angle.
- IV is true because C=sin^{-1}(1/n) for a medium surrounded by air.

Therefore, I, II and IV are correct.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2007 — Laws of refraction
question: Which statement correctly expresses Snell's law for light travelling from medium 1 into medium 2?

options.text: dfrac{sin r}{sin i} is always equal to 1.
dfrac{sin i}{sin r} is constant for a given pair of media and wavelength, and equals the refractive index of medium 2 relative to medium 1.
dfrac{i}{r} is always equal to the absolute refractive index of medium 2.
The ratio sin i/sin r changes whenever the angle of incidence changes, even for the same pair of media.

explanation: Snell's law gives n_{21}=sin i/sin r. The ratio of the angles themselves is not generally equal to the refractive index. The ratio of the sines remains constant for a fixed pair of media and wavelength.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2007 — Plane mirror versus total internal reflection
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes ordinary reflection at a plane mirror from total internal reflection at a suitable prism face?

options.text: A plane mirror always reflects all incident light, while total internal reflection absorbs it.
Total internal reflection requires light to travel from a rarer to a denser medium.
A plane mirror and total internal reflection always reflect exactly the same fraction of incident light.
Under ideal conditions, total internal reflection reflects the incident light back into the denser medium, whereas an ordinary mirror can have losses through absorption and transmission.

explanation: Total internal reflection ideally reflects essentially all incident optical energy back into the denser medium. Real mirrors can absorb some light, and a glass mirror may transmit some light through its surfaces. The distinction is not that total internal reflection requires a rarer-to-denser transition.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2008 — Speed and wavelength in glass
question: A monochromatic beam of wavelength lambda in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The speed in glass is c/1.5, the wavelength becomes lambda/1.5, and the frequency remains unchanged.
The speed becomes 1.5c, and the wavelength remains unchanged.
The speed remains c, while the frequency decreases by a factor of 1.5.
Both the frequency and wavelength decrease by a factor of 1.5.

explanation: The refractive index is n=c/v, so v=c/1.5. Since frequency is unchanged and v=flambda, the wavelength becomes lambda/1.5. The speed cannot increase to 1.5c.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2009 — Conditions for total internal reflection
question: Which pair of conditions is necessary for total internal reflection?

options.text: Light travels from a rarer to a denser medium at any incidence angle.
Light strikes the interface normally while travelling from glass to air.
Light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
The angle of refraction must be smaller than the angle of incidence in every situation.

explanation: Both conditions must be satisfied: the light must approach from the denser medium, and its incidence angle must be greater than the critical angle. At normal incidence, total internal reflection does not occur.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2010 — Critical angle in a glass slab
question: A glass slab has a critical angle of 42^° for a glass–air interface. A ray inside the glass strikes that interface at 45^°. What happens?

options.text: It refracts into air at 45^°.
It undergoes total internal reflection because 45^°>42^°.
It refracts into air at 90^° because its incidence angle exceeds the critical angle.
It passes normally into air because the critical angle is approximately 45^°.

explanation: Since the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle, total internal reflection occurs. At exactly 42^°, the refracted ray would graze the interface; at 45^°, there is no ordinary propagating refracted ray in air.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2014 — Glass slab versus triangular prism
question: A ray passes through a rectangular glass slab and then through a triangular glass prism, each surrounded by air. Which statement correctly compares their emergent directions?

options.text: Both emergent rays are necessarily parallel to their respective incident rays.
The slab causes angular deviation, but the prism produces only lateral displacement.
Neither produces any change in the ray's direction.
The slab's emergent ray is parallel to its incident ray, whereas the prism generally produces angular deviation because its refracting faces are not parallel.

explanation: Parallel slab faces cancel the angular deviation, although lateral displacement remains. A prism has inclined faces, so the angular changes generally do not cancel. The emergent ray is therefore generally not parallel to the incident ray.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2015 — Lateral displacement
question: Which change can increase the lateral displacement of a ray passing through a parallel-sided glass slab, with other relevant conditions suitably fixed?

options.text: Increasing the slab thickness.
Making the refractive index of the slab exactly equal to that of air.
Reducing the thickness to zero.
Making the ray incident normally and retaining the same slab.

explanation: Lateral displacement is proportional to slab thickness for fixed incidence angle and refractive index. Normal incidence gives zero lateral displacement, and a medium with the same refractive index as air produces no refraction at the interface.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Previous Board Question, 2018 — Critical angle and colour
question: For ordinary transparent glass in the visible range, which statement is generally correct when comparing red and green light?

options.text: Red light has a smaller critical angle because its refractive index is lower.
Both colours must have identical critical angles because they travel in the same glass.
Red light generally has a larger critical angle because its refractive index is lower than that of green light.
Green light has a larger critical angle because its wavelength is shorter.

explanation: In ordinary glass, refractive index generally decreases as wavelength increases. Red light has a longer wavelength and lower refractive index than green light, so C=sin^{-1}(1/n) is larger for red light.

title: Cause of refraction
question: A light ray crosses obliquely from air into glass. Which statement most accurately explains the physical cause of its change in direction?

options.text: The frequency of light increases suddenly as it enters glass.
The speed of light changes at the boundary, causing the ray to change direction when it enters obliquely.
The light ray experiences a gravitational force towards the normal.
The wavelength remains constant while the frequency decreases.

explanation: The speed of light changes when it enters a medium of different refractive index. At oblique incidence, this change in speed causes the ray to change direction. Frequency remains unchanged at the boundary, while wavelength changes.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Assertion–Reason: Frequency during refraction
question: Assertion (A):** The frequency of monochromatic light remains unchanged when it passes from air into glass. **Reason (R):** The frequency is determined by the source, and the wave oscillations must remain continuous across the stationary boundary.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Frequency during refraction

**Assertion (A):** The frequency of monochromatic light remains unchanged when it passes from air into glass.

**Reason (R):** The frequency is determined by the source, and the wave oscillations must remain continuous across the stationary boundary.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** The frequency remains constant across a stationary interface. The speed and wavelength change to satisfy v=flambda. Both statements are true, and the reason explains the assertion.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Laws of refraction
question: Which statement correctly describes the two laws of refraction?

options.text: The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in different planes, and the angles of incidence and refraction are always equal.
The angle of incidence is proportional to the angle of refraction for every pair of media.
The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane; for a given pair of media and wavelength, sin i/sin r is constant.
The refractive index depends only on the angle of incidence and not on the media.

explanation: The first law states that the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane. The second law, Snell's law, states that the ratio sin i/sin r remains constant for a given pair of media and wavelength.

title: Absolute and relative refractive index
question: The absolute refractive indices of media P and Q are 1.8 and 1.2, respectively. Which statement is correct?

The refractive index of P relative to Q is 0.67.
The speed of light in P is greater than that in Q.
The refractive index of P relative to Q is 1.5, and light travels more slowly in P.

explanation:
n_{PQ}=(n_P / n_Q)
=(1.8 / 1.2)=1.5


Since v=c/n, light travels more slowly in P. Option A reverses the relative refractive-index ratio.

title: Why does a ray incident normally suffer no deviation?
question: A ray enters a rectangular glass slab normally. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Glass has the same refractive index as air at normal incidence.
The ray has zero angle of incidence, so Snell's law gives zero angle of refraction, although speed and wavelength change.
Normal incidence prevents the speed of light from changing.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at both surfaces.

explanation:
is correct?

A) Glass has the same refractive index as air at normal incidence.

B) The ray has zero angle of incidence, so Snell's law gives zero angle of refraction, although speed and wavelength change.

C) Normal incidence prevents the speed of light from changing.

D) The ray undergoes total internal reflection at both surfaces.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:** At normal incidence, i=0^°. Snell's law gives r=0^°, so there is no directional deviation. The ray still travels more slowly in glass and has a shorter wavelength.

title: Rectangular glass slab
question: Which statement about a ray passing through a parallel-sided glass slab surrounded by air is correct?

options.text: The emergent ray is generally parallel to the incident ray but may be laterally displaced.
The emergent ray is always perpendicular to the incident ray.
The emergent ray is always coincident with the incident ray, irrespective of incidence angle and slab thickness.
The emergent ray must travel towards the normal at the second surface.

explanation: The two slab surfaces are parallel. The angular deviation at the first surface is cancelled by the opposite deviation at the second surface. A lateral displacement generally remains for oblique incidence.

title: Factors affecting lateral displacement
question: For a fixed refractive index and fixed angle of incidence, what happens to the lateral displacement through a parallel-sided glass slab when its thickness is doubled?

options.text: It becomes half.
It remains unchanged.
It becomes twice as large.
It becomes four times as large.

explanation:
The lateral displacement is


d=t(sin(i-r) / cos r)


For fixed i and r, displacement is directly proportional to slab thickness t. Doubling the thickness doubles the displacement.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Apparent depth
question: An object is viewed vertically from air through a transparent liquid. Which statement is correct for near-normal viewing?

options.text: Apparent depth is always greater than real depth.
Apparent depth is equal to real depth multiplied by the refractive index.
Apparent depth is independent of the refractive index.
Apparent depth equals real depth divided by the refractive index of the liquid relative to air.

concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Apparent shift
question: Which change increases the apparent upward shift of an object viewed normally from air through a liquid, assuming the real depth remains fixed?

options.text: Increasing the refractive index of the liquid.
Decreasing the refractive index of the liquid towards 1.
Reducing the real depth to zero.
Making the refractive index of the liquid equal to that of air.

explanation:
Shift=d_{real}≤ft(1-frac1nright)


For fixed real depth, increasing n increases the apparent shift. When n=1, there is no apparent shift.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction from denser to rarer medium
question: A ray travels from glass into air at an incidence angle smaller than the critical angle. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Total internal reflection must occur because glass is denser.
The ray refracts into air, bending away from the normal.
The ray bends towards the normal because its speed increases.
The ray cannot cross the boundary unless the incidence angle is 90^°.

explanation: When light travels from glass to air below the critical angle, it refracts into air and bends away from the normal. Total internal reflection requires an incidence angle greater than the critical angle, not merely a denser incident medium.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Critical angle
question: Which statement correctly defines the critical angle?

options.text: The angle between the incident ray and the surface when the refracted ray is normal to the surface.
The angle of refraction when the incident angle is 90^°.
The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90^°.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal during ordinary reflection.

explanation: At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the interface. Its angle with the normal is 90^°. The critical angle itself is measured inside the denser medium.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Conditions for total internal reflection
question: Which combination is necessary for total internal reflection at a boundary?

options.text: Light travels from a rarer to a denser medium at any angle.
Light travels from a denser to a rarer medium, but its incidence angle is below the critical angle.
Light travels normally from glass into air.
Light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, with incidence angle greater than the critical angle.

explanation: Both conditions are necessary: light must approach the boundary from the optically denser medium, and the incidence angle must exceed the critical angle. Neither condition alone is sufficient.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refractive index and critical angle
question: Two transparent media are surrounded by air. Medium P has a critical angle of 30^°, while medium Q has a critical angle of 45^°. Which statement is correct?

options.text: P has a higher refractive index than Q.
Q has a higher refractive index than P.
Both have equal refractive indices because both critical rays travel along the boundary.
The refractive index cannot be compared using critical angles.

explanation:
n=frac1{sin C}


A smaller critical angle corresponds to a higher refractive index when the surrounding medium is the same. Therefore, P has the higher refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Assertion–Reason: Total internal reflection
question: Assertion (A):** A ray travelling from glass into air at an incidence angle greater than the critical angle undergoes total internal reflection. **Reason (R):** At such an angle, Snell's law would require the sine of the refracted angle to exceed 1.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Total internal reflection

**Assertion (A):** A ray travelling from glass into air at an incidence angle greater than the critical angle undergoes total internal reflection.

**Reason (R):** At such an angle, Snell's law would require the sine of the refracted angle to exceed 1.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** For incidence beyond the critical angle, Snell's law cannot give a real refracted angle because it would require sin r>1. No ordinary refracted ray propagates into the rarer medium, so total internal reflection occurs.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Optical fibres
question: Why does a conventional optical fibre have a core of higher refractive index than its cladding?

options.text: To make the frequency of light increase in the core.
To ensure light travels faster in the core than in the cladding.
To permit total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface for suitable internal incidence angles.
To prevent the wavelength from changing when light enters the core.

explanation: A higher-index core surrounded by lower-index cladding permits total internal reflection when the internal incidence angle exceeds the critical angle. This guides light along the fibre.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Right-angled prism
question: A right-angled isosceles glass prism is used to deviate a ray through 90^° by total internal reflection. Which condition is essential at the reflecting face?

options.text: The ray must strike the face normally.
The internal angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle for the glass–surrounding-medium pair.
The prism must have a refractive index equal to 1.
The ray must enter the prism from air at 90^° to the surface.

explanation: The ray must undergo total internal reflection at the reflecting face. Therefore, the internal incidence angle must exceed the critical angle, and the surrounding medium must be optically rarer than the prism.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Sparkling of diamonds
question: Which property contributes most directly to the repeated total internal reflections responsible for the brilliance of a properly cut diamond?

options.text: Its refractive index is approximately equal to that of air.
Its critical angle is very large.
Its light absorption is necessarily complete.
Its high refractive index produces a small critical angle.

explanation: Diamond has a refractive index of approximately 2.42, giving a critical angle of about 24.4^° in air. Many rays undergo repeated internal reflection before emerging through suitable facets.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Mirage formation
question: Which explanation best describes a common inferior mirage seen over a hot road?

options.text: Temperature-dependent atmospheric refraction bends rays through layers of varying refractive index, sometimes with total internal reflection contributing to the ray path.
The road produces a real pool of water through condensation.
Light travels in a perfectly straight line through every atmospheric layer.
The phenomenon is caused by the complete absorption of light by hot air.

explanation:
best describes a common inferior mirage seen over a hot road?

A) Temperature-dependent atmospheric refraction bends rays through layers of varying refractive index, sometimes with total internal reflection contributing to the ray path.

B) The road produces a real pool of water through condensation.

C) Light travels in a perfectly straight line through every atmospheric layer.

D) The phenomenon is caused by the complete absorption of light by hot air.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Air near the hot road is generally less dense and has a lower refractive index than the cooler air above. The refractive-index gradient bends rays and can produce an apparent image resembling water.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Twinkling of stars
question: Why do stars appear to twinkle?

options.text: Their emitted frequency changes randomly every second.
Atmospheric turbulence continually changes the refraction of their light, causing fluctuations in apparent brightness and position.
Their light undergoes total internal reflection at every atmospheric layer.
Earth's rotation changes the frequency of the light reaching the observer.

explanation: Atmospheric refractive-index variations cause changing ray paths and brightness. Stars appear nearly point-like, making these fluctuations noticeable.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Advanced sunrise and delayed sunset
question: Which statement explains why the Sun can remain visible when its geometric position is slightly below the horizon?

options.text: The atmosphere makes the Sun physically rise earlier.
The atmosphere reflects sunlight only by ordinary mirror reflection.
Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight so that the apparent position of the Sun is higher than its geometric position.
Light travels faster in the lower atmosphere and is therefore accelerated upwards.

explanation: Atmospheric layers have different refractive indices. The curved ray path makes the Sun appear higher than its true geometric position, causing advanced sunrise and delayed sunset.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction and wavelength
question: Which statement about monochromatic light entering glass from air is correct?

options.text: Its speed decreases, its wavelength decreases, and its frequency remains unchanged.
Its speed increases, its wavelength decreases, and its frequency remains unchanged.
Its speed decreases, its frequency increases, and its wavelength remains unchanged.
Its speed and wavelength remain unchanged, but its frequency decreases.

explanation: The refractive index of glass exceeds that of air, so v=c/n decreases. Frequency remains constant at the boundary, and lambda=v/f decreases as well.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Which statement is incorrect?
question: Which statement is incorrect?

options.text: A ray entering a denser medium obliquely generally bends towards the normal.
The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that medium.
The emergent ray from a parallel-sided slab in the same external medium is parallel to the incident ray.
Total internal reflection occurs whenever light crosses from any medium into a medium with a different refractive index.

explanation: Total internal reflection does not occur at every refractive boundary. It requires light to travel from denser to rarer medium with an incidence angle greater than the critical angle.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Matching: Optical phenomenon and explanation
question: Which matching is entirely correct?

options.text: Twinkling of stars — dispersion inside a glass prism.
Advanced sunrise — total internal reflection at the ocean surface.
Apparent depth — backward extensions of refracted rays locate a virtual image closer to the surface.
Diamond brilliance — the frequency of light increases during each internal reflection.

explanation:
Which matching is entirely correct?

A) Twinkling of stars — dispersion inside a glass prism.

B) Advanced sunrise — total internal reflection at the ocean surface.

C) Apparent depth — backward extensions of refracted rays locate a virtual image closer to the surface.

D) Diamond brilliance — the frequency of light increases during each internal reflection.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** Apparent depth arises because refracted rays entering air are traced backwards to an apparent image. The other options confuse unrelated phenomena or incorrectly describe the physics.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Assertion–Reason: Apparent depth
question: Assertion (A):** A coin at the bottom of a water-filled vessel appears raised when viewed nearly normally from air. **Reason (R):** Light from the coin bends away from the normal when it travels from water into air.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Apparent depth

**Assertion (A):** A coin at the bottom of a water-filled vessel appears raised when viewed nearly normally from air.

**Reason (R):** Light from the coin bends away from the normal when it travels from water into air.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Light bends away from the normal as it enters air from water. The eye traces the refracted rays backwards, placing the apparent image above the real coin.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why frequency remains constant
question: A light ray enters glass from air. Which statement best explains why its frequency does not change?

options.text: Glass and air have the same refractive index.
The boundary changes the propagation speed and wavelength, but the oscillation frequency remains fixed by the source and boundary continuity.
Frequency is proportional to the refractive index of every medium.
The ray stops oscillating momentarily at the boundary.

explanation: The source determines the frequency. At a stationary boundary, frequency remains continuous while the speed and wavelength adjust to the new medium.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: A ray incident at the critical angle
question: A ray travels from glass into air at exactly the critical angle. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It undergoes total internal reflection with no refracted ray at all.
It refracts towards the normal with angle 0^°.
Its incident angle is 90^°, and its refracted angle is the critical angle.
Its refracted ray travels along the interface, making 90^° with the normal.

explanation: At the critical angle, the refracted angle is 90^°. Total internal reflection occurs only when the incidence angle is greater than the critical angle.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why a parallel-sided slab does not produce angular deviation
question: Which factor is responsible for the emergent ray being parallel to the incident ray through a rectangular glass slab surrounded by air?

options.text: The refractive index of glass is always exactly 1.5.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at both slab surfaces.
The opposite angular deviations at the two parallel surfaces cancel.
The incident ray must always be perpendicular to the slab.

explanation: Parallel faces have parallel normals. Refraction at the second surface reverses the angular change introduced at the first, restoring the original direction while generally leaving lateral displacement.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Relative refractive index
question: The refractive index of medium B relative to medium A is less than 1. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Light travels faster in B than in A.
Light must undergo total internal reflection while travelling from A to B.
Medium B must be opaque.
Light travels more slowly in B than in A.

explanation:
For transparent media,


n_{BA}=(v_A / v_B)


If n_{BA}<1, then v_B>v_A. This does not by itself guarantee total internal reflection; the direction and angle of incidence also matter.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction through a layered medium
question: Light travels from medium A into B and then into C through parallel interfaces. The refractive indices are 1.0, 1.5, and 1.2, respectively. Which statement is correct if the ray crosses both interfaces without total internal reflection?

options.text: The ray's frequency increases in B and decreases in C.
The ray bends towards the normal in B and then away from the normal in C; its final angle depends on the refractive index of C relative to A.
The ray must emerge parallel to its original direction because all interfaces are parallel, regardless of the final medium.
The ray's speed is the same in all three media.

explanation: Entry from A into higher-index B causes bending towards the normal. Entry from B into lower-index C causes bending away from the normal. Since C has a different refractive index from A, the final direction need not match the original direction. Frequency remains unchanged throughout.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Evaluating statements about refraction
question: Consider the following statements: I. A refracted ray may bend towards or away from the normal, depending on the media and direction of travel. II. The refractive index of a medium is dimensionless. III. At normal incidence, the ray changes direction but not speed. IV. A critical angle exists for light travelling from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium. Which combination is correct?

options.text: I and III only.
II and III only.
I, II and IV only.
I, II, III and IV.

explanation: Statements I, II and IV are correct. Statement III is false: at normal incidence the ray does not change direction, but its speed generally changes when the refractive index changes.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Determining the angle of incidence from a refracted ray
question: A ray travels from air into a transparent medium of refractive index 1.4. If the angle of refraction is 30^°, calculate the angle of incidence.
explanation:
By Snell's law,


sin i=1.4sin30^°=0.7


Therefore,


i=sin^{-1}(0.7)≈44.4^°


Option A results from taking the inverse sine of the wrong ratio.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comparing light speeds in two media
question: The speed of light in medium A is 2.5×10^8 m/s, while that in medium B is 2.0×10^8 m/s. What is the refractive index of B relative to A?
explanation:
The relative refractive index of B with respect to A is


n_{BA}=(v_A / v_B)



n_{BA}=(2.5 / 2.0)=1.25


The relative refractive index is the inverse of the speed ratio. Option A gives v_B/v_A.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Apparent depth in a two-layer liquid tank
question: A tank contains two transparent liquid layers, each 6 cm thick. Their refractive indices are 1.2 and 1.5, respectively. A small object lies at the bottom. Viewed vertically from air, what is the apparent depth of the object below the top surface?

options.text: 12 cm
9 cm
8 cm
5 cm

explanation:
For near-normal viewing through plane-parallel layers, the apparent depth is the sum of the apparent thicknesses:


d_{app}=(6 / 1.2)+(6 / 1.5)



d_{app}=5+4=9 cm


**Correction:** The correct answer is **B, 9 cm**. Option C incorrectly combines the layers using an inappropriate single refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Determining whether total internal reflection occurs
question: A ray inside glass of refractive index 1.6 strikes a glass–air boundary at 40^°. What happens at the boundary?

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs because the incidence angle exceeds 30^°.
The ray emerges into air at exactly 90^°.
The ray emerges into air at an angle smaller than 40^°.
The ray refracts into air at an angle greater than 40^° but less than 90^°.

explanation:
The critical angle is


C=sin^{-1}≤ft(frac1{1.6}right)
≈38.7^°


Since 40^°>C, the ray undergoes total internal reflection.

**Correction:** The correct physical conclusion is total internal reflection, so **A should be the correct option**, with the explanation revised to state that the critical angle is approximately 38.7^°.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding the refractive index from a speed ratio
question: The speed of light in a transparent material is 75% of its speed in vacuum. What is the absolute refractive index of the material?
explanation:
Given v=0.75c,


n=(c / v)=(c / 0.75c)
=frac1{0.75}=1.33


Option A gives v/c, the reciprocal of the refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Time taken by light to cross a glass slab
question: A light ray travels normally through a glass slab 30 cm thick. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5. How long does the ray take to cross the slab?
explanation:
The speed in glass is


v=(3×10^8 / 1.5)
=2×10^8 m/s


The thickness is 0.30 m, so


t=(0.30 / 2×10^8)
=1.5×10^{-9} s


Option D incorrectly uses the speed of light in vacuum.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Lateral displacement with a different slab thickness
question: A ray passes through a parallel-sided slab of thickness 6 cm. The angle of incidence is 45^°, and the angle of refraction is 30^°. Calculate the lateral displacement.
explanation:
d=t(sin(i-r) / cos r)



d=6(sin15^° / cos30^°)



d=6(0.2588 / 0.8660)
≈1.79 cm


**Correction:** The calculated displacement is approximately 1.79 cm, so none of the options is exact. Option A should be revised to 1.79 cm.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding apparent shift from apparent depth
question: A coin is placed at the bottom of a liquid. Its apparent depth is 16 cm, while the liquid has a refractive index of 1.25. What is the apparent upward shift?

options.text: 4 cm
3.2 cm
20 cm
5 cm

explanation:
First calculate the real depth:


d_{real}=n,d_{app}
=1.25×16=20 cm


Then,


Shift=20-16=4 cm


Option C gives the real depth rather than the shift.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refracted angle in a denser medium
question: Light enters a medium of refractive index 1.8 from air at an incidence angle of 30^°. Calculate the angle of refraction.
explanation:
sin r=(sin30^° / 1.8)
=(0.5 / 1.8)=0.2778



r=sin^{-1}(0.2778)≈16.1^°


Option D incorrectly predicts bending away from the normal.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding the wavelength in a liquid from the speed
question: The frequency of light remains 5×10^ Hz as it enters a liquid where its speed is 2.25×10^8 m/s. What is its wavelength in the liquid?

options.text: 450 nm
500 nm
600 nm
750 nm

explanation:
lambda=(v / f)
=(2.25×10^8 / 5×10^{14)}



lambda=4.5×10^{-7} m=450 nm


Option B corresponds to the wavelength in vacuum for this frequency.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comparing apparent shifts in two media
question: Two liquids have refractive indices 1.25 and 1.6. Objects are placed at the same real depth of 16 cm in both liquids and viewed normally from air. What is the difference in their apparent shifts?

options.text: 1.6 cm
2.8 cm
3.5 cm
4.0 cm

explanation:
For the first liquid,


d₁=(16 / 1.25)=12.8 cm


Shift =16-12.8=3.2 cm.

For the second liquid,


d₂=(16 / 1.6)=10 cm


Shift =16-10=6 cm.

Difference:


6-3.2=2.8 cm
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refractive index of B relative to A using their speeds
question: Light travels at 2.4×10^8 m/s in medium A and 1.8×10^8 m/s in medium B. Calculate the refractive index of B relative to A.
explanation:
n_{BA}=(v_A / v_B)
=(2.4 / 1.8)=1.33


Option A uses the reciprocal ratio.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Critical angle when the refractive index is √(2)
question: A transparent medium has refractive index √(2) relative to air. Calculate its critical angle.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comparing speeds using critical angles
question: Two transparent media P and Q have critical angles 30^° and 45^°, respectively, when surrounded by air. What is the ratio of the speed of light in P to that in Q?

options.text: 1:sqrt2
1:sqrt3
sqrt2:1

explanation:
The absolute refractive index is n=1/sin C, and speed is inversely proportional to refractive index. Thus,


(v_P / v_Q)=(n_Q / n_P)
=(1/sin45^° / 1/sin30^°)



(v_P / v_Q)=(0.5 / 0.7071)
=frac1{sqrt2}


**Correction:** The ratio is 1:sqrt2, so **A is the correct answer**.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Determining real depth from refractive index and shift
question: A submerged object has an apparent upward shift of 5 cm. The liquid's refractive index is 1.25. Calculate the real depth.

options.text: 20 cm
25 cm
15 cm

explanation:
Let the real depth be d. Then


d_{app}=(d / 1.25)


The apparent shift is


d-(d / 1.25)=5



d-0.8d=5



0.2d=5Rightarrow d=25 cm


**Correction:** The correct answer is **B, 25 cm**.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Calculating the refractive index from a critical angle and speed
question: A transparent medium has a critical angle of 45^° when surrounded by air. Calculate the speed of light in the medium.
explanation:
n=frac1{sin45^°}=sqrt2


Therefore,


v=(c / n)
=(3×10^8 / sqrt2)
≈2.12×10^8 m/s
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Two-stage refraction through different media
question: Light travels from air into medium A with refractive index 1.5, and then into medium B with refractive index 1.2. The two interfaces are parallel. If the angle of incidence in air is 60^°, calculate the angle the ray makes with the normal inside medium B.
explanation:
For parallel interfaces, Snell's law gives the same value of nsintheta at each interface:


1sin60^°=1.2sin r_B


Therefore,


sin r_B=(0.8660 / 1.2)=0.7217



r_B≈46.2^°


**Correction:** The calculated angle is approximately 46.2^°, not 54.7^°. The correct option should be revised to 46.2^°.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Calculating apparent shift inside a glass block
question: A glass block has a thickness of 18 cm and a refractive index of 1.5. Viewed normally from air, what is the apparent upward shift of its lower surface?

options.text: 6 cm
9 cm
12 cm
15 cm

explanation:
The apparent thickness is


t'=(t / n)=(18 / 1.5)=12 cm


The apparent shift is


t-t'=18-12=6 cm


**Correction:** The correct answer is **A, 6 cm**. Option B incorrectly confuses apparent thickness with apparent shift.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding the critical angle from a measured speed
question: Light travels through a transparent material at 2×10^8 m/s. The material is surrounded by air. What is its critical angle?
explanation:
First find the refractive index:


n=(c / v)=(3×10^8 / 2×10^8)=1.5


Then,


sin C=frac1{1.5}=frac23



C≈41.8^°
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding the wavelength in a transparent medium
question: Light of frequency 6×10^ Hz travels through glass of refractive index 1.5. What is its wavelength in glass?

options.text: 500 nm
333 nm
750 nm
250 nm

explanation:
The speed in glass is


v=(3×10^8 / 1.5)=2×10^8 m/s


Therefore,


lambda=(v / f)
=(2×10^8 / 6×10^{14)}
=3.33×10^{-7} m


Thus,


lambda≈333 nm


Option A corresponds approximately to the wavelength in vacuum, not in glass.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Calculating the angle of refraction in water
question: Light travels from air into water with an angle of incidence of 45^°. The refractive index of water is 4/3. Calculate the angle of refraction, approximately.
explanation:
Using Snell's law,


sin r=(sin45^° / 4/3)
=(0.7071×3 / 4)=0.5303


Therefore,


r=sin^{-1}(0.5303)≈32.0^°


Option C ignores refraction, while D predicts bending in the wrong direction.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding the real depth of a swimming pool
question: A swimming pool appears to be 2.4 m deep when viewed vertically from above. The refractive index of water is 4/3. Calculate the actual depth.
explanation:
n=(real depth / apparent depth)


Hence,


Real depth=frac43×2.4
=3.2 m


Option A incorrectly divides the apparent depth by the refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Wavelength of light inside glass
question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. What is its wavelength in glass?

options.text: 900 nm
600 nm
300 nm
400 nm

explanation:
Frequency remains unchanged, so wavelength is inversely proportional to refractive index:

diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="48" width="300" height="142" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.18" /><path d="M10 48 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><circle cx="95" cy="150" r="5" fill="#D97706" /><circle cx="230" cy="150" r="5" fill="#0D9488" /><circle cx="95" cy="124" r="4" fill="#D97706" fill-opacity="0.6" /><circle cx="230" cy="114" r="4" fill="#0D9488" fill-opacity="0.6" /><path d="M95 150 L140 48 L183 18 M230 150 L265 48 L291 18" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 3" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><text x="15" y="30" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="15" y="68" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="105" y="128" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Image A</text><text x="238" y="111" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Image B</text><text x="65" y="174" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Object A</text><text x="200" y="174" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Object B</text></svg>

options.text: A: 8 cm; B: 12 cm
A: 6 cm; B: 9 cm
A: 2 cm; B: 3 cm

explanation:
For near-normal viewing,


d_{apparent}=frac{d_{real}}{n}


For A,


d_A=(8 / 4/3)=6 cm


For B,


d_B=(12 / 4/3)=9 cm


Both objects appear raised towards the surface. Option A reverses the real-to-apparent depth ratio.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Relative refractive index from two absolute indices
question: The ray crosses media with known absolute refractive indices; the question concerns B relative to A. The absolute refractive indices of media A and B are 1.50 and 1.25, respectively. What is the refractive index of B relative to A?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="10" width="296" height="48" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity="0.15" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><rect x="12" y="60" width="296" height="48" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><rect x="12" y="110" width="296" height="58" fill="#0D9488" fill-opacity="0.12" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="24" y="29" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air: n = 1</text><text x="24" y="79" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium A: n = 1.5</text><text x="24" y="132" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium B: n = 1.25</text><path d="M80 16 L110 60 L123 108 L139 160" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M139 160 L134 151 M139 160 L145 152" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /></svg>
explanation:
The relative refractive index of B with respect to A is


n_{BA}=(n_B / n_A)
=(1.25 / 1.50)
=frac56≈0.833


Option A gives the reciprocal, n_{AB}, rather than B relative to A.
