chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comparing incidence angle with the critical angle
question: A ray is incident from glass of refractive index 1.5 into air at 40^°. The critical angle for the glass–air interface is approximately 41.8^°. The incident ray makes an angle of 40^° with the normal. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="8" y="90" width="304" height="78" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M8 90 H312 M160 15 V168" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M55 145 L160 90 L244 32" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M160 90 L244 32" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="18" y="110" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Glass</text><text x="18" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="168" y="26" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="75" y="130" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = 40°</text><text x="220" y="24" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Refracted ray</text></svg>

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs because 40^° is close to the critical angle.
The ray is reflected completely because the incident medium is glass.
The refracted angle is 41.8^°.
The ray refracts into air at an angle greater than 40^°, but less than 90^°.

explanation:
Since 40^°<41.8^°, total internal reflection does not occur. By Snell's law,


1.5sin40^°=sin r



sin r≈0.9642


Therefore, r≈74.6^°, which is greater than 40^° but less than 90^°. Option A incorrectly assumes that being close to the critical angle is sufficient for total internal reflection.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Identifying the ray path at a critical-angle boundary
question: The incident ray is inside the denser medium; the refracted ray travels along the interface. A ray strikes a glass–air interface at its critical angle. Which statement correctly distinguishes this situation from total internal reflection?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="90" width="300" height="75" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M10 90 H310 M160 15 V165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M65 145 L160 90 L278 90" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M266 83 L278 90 L266 97" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="111" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Denser medium</text><text x="18" y="22" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Rarer medium</text><text x="174" y="79" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">r = 90°</text><text x="81" y="130" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = C</text></svg>

options.text: At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the interface; total internal reflection occurs when the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle.
At the critical angle, the incident ray travels along the interface, while the refracted ray returns into glass.
At the critical angle, the refracted ray bends towards the normal and enters air.
At the critical angle, both the incident and refracted rays make angles of 90^° with the normal.

explanation: At the critical angle, the angle of refraction is 90^°. The incident angle itself is less than 90^°. Total internal reflection begins when the incidence angle is greater than the critical angle. Option D confuses the incident angle with the refracted angle.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Choosing the correct prism arrangement for deviation
question: Arrangement I Arrangement II Both arrangements use a right-angled isosceles prism. The intended internal incidence at the hypotenuse is 45^°. A glass prism has refractive index 1.5. A ray enters normally through one short face and strikes the hypotenuse at 45^°. Which statement about using the prism as a reflector is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 120" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 100 L20 20 L120 100 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" /><path d="M2 65 L20 65 L20 100" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M20 65 L58 65 L58 25" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><text x="24" y="112" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Right angle</text></svg>

options.text: The prism cannot reflect the ray internally because a glass surface always refracts light into air.
The prism can act as a reflector because 45^° exceeds the glass–air critical angle, so total internal reflection occurs at the hypotenuse.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection only when the hypotenuse is parallel to the incident ray.
The ray emerges undeviated through the hypotenuse because the incident ray entered normally through another face.

explanation:
For glass of refractive index 1.5,


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 1.5)right)
≈41.8^°


Since 45^°>C, total internal reflection occurs at the hypotenuse. A right-angled isosceles prism can therefore change the direction of a ray by 90^° in this arrangement.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction through a prism versus a rectangular slab
question: Parallel slab Triangular prism The slab has parallel faces; the prism has non-parallel refracting faces. A ray passes obliquely through a rectangular glass slab and then through a triangular glass prism of the same material. Which difference is expected when both are surrounded by air and total internal reflection is absent?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 115" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="30" y="15" width="80" height="85" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M3 85 L30 64 L110 42 L137 21" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M3 85 L30 64 L110 42 L137 21" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /></svg>

options.text: Both emergent rays must be parallel to their respective incident rays.
The slab produces angular deviation but no lateral displacement, whereas the prism produces neither.
The slab's emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, whereas the prism generally produces an angular deviation because its refracting faces are not parallel.
The prism produces no refraction because the two faces have different orientations.

explanation: A parallel-sided slab produces equal and opposite angular changes at its two surfaces, leaving the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced. A triangular prism has non-parallel refracting faces, so the deviations generally do not cancel. Option A incorrectly applies the slab result to a prism.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Identifying the correct ray diagram for an apparent image
question: The apparent image is obtained by extending the refracted rays backwards into the water. A student draws the backward extension of a refracted ray from a submerged object and places the apparent image below the real object. Which correction is necessary for near-normal viewing from air into water?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="70" width="300" height="120" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.18" /><path d="M10 70 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><circle cx="125" cy="155" r="5" fill="#D97706" /><circle cx="125" cy="134" r="4" fill="#0D9488" /><path d="M125 155 L177 70 L235 20" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M177 70 L235 20" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M125 155 L235 20" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 4" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="23" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="18" y="89" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="134" y="130" font-size="10" fill="#0D9488">Apparent image</text><text x="134" y="170" font-size="10" fill="#D97706">Real object</text><text x="238" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Eye</text></svg>

options.text: Move the apparent image closer to the water surface because the object appears shallower than it really is.
Move the apparent image deeper because refraction always increases apparent depth.
Place the apparent image exactly on the water surface, irrespective of the object's depth.
Remove the backward extension because a virtual image cannot be formed by refraction.

explanation: When light travels from water to air, it bends away from the normal. The eye traces the refracted rays backwards in straight lines, locating a virtual image closer to the surface than the real object. Option B reverses the direction of the apparent shift.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Optical fibre with the wrong refractive-index arrangement
question: The proposed fibre has a core of lower refractive index than its surrounding cladding. A student proposes an optical fibre with core refractive index 1.40 and cladding refractive index 1.50. The diagram shows light zigzagging inside the core by total internal reflection. What is the fundamental problem?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="35" width="296" height="100" rx="4" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><rect x="12" y="57" width="296" height="56" rx="2" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.25" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M18 85 L68 60 L118 108 L168 60 L218 108 L280 85" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="26" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Cladding: n = 1.50</text><text x="18" y="76" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Core: n = 1.40</text><text x="18" y="153" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Proposed fibre arrangement</text></svg>

options.text: The refractive index of the core must be exactly 1.
Total internal reflection is impossible at every interface between transparent materials.
The refractive index of the cladding must be lower than that of the core for the intended guiding mechanism; the proposed arrangement cannot support that mechanism at the core–cladding boundary.
The speed of light must be higher in the cladding than in a vacuum.

explanation: For conventional step-index optical fibre guiding, the core must have a higher refractive index than the cladding. The ray travelling in the core must encounter a boundary leading to a lower-index medium to undergo total internal reflection. Here, the cladding has the higher index, so the proposed ray path is not supported by the intended mechanism.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Explaining the formation of a mirage
question: Air close to a hot road is generally hotter and less optically dense than the air above it. A driver sees what appears to be a pool of water on a hot road, but no water is present. Which explanation best matches the ray diagram?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 155 H312" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" /><path d="M8 132 Q80 120 160 132 T312 132" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><path d="M8 105 Q80 94 160 105 T312 105" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><circle cx="48" cy="42" r="6" fill="#F59E0B" /><circle cx="48" cy="42" r="6" fill="#F59E0B" /><path d="M48 42 Q100 63 140 95 Q180 130 240 125" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M240 125 L230 119 M240 125 L232 132" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M240 125 L290 66" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 4" fill="none" /><text x="13" y="23" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Distant object</text><text x="13" y="171" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Hot road surface</text><text x="180" y="91" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Curved ray path</text><text x="220" y="153" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Apparent image</text></svg>

options.text: Water vapour forms a real reflecting pool on the road.

Light from the sky curves through atmospheric layers of varying refractive index; under suitable conditions, strong bending and total internal reflection near the hot surface can contribute to the apparent image.
The road emits blue light because its temperature is high.
The phenomenon occurs because the refractive index of air is zero near the road.

explanation:
best matches the ray diagram?

A) Water vapour forms a real reflecting pool on the road.

B) Light from the sky curves through atmospheric layers of varying refractive index; under suitable conditions, strong bending and total internal reflection near the hot surface can contribute to the apparent image.

C) The road emits blue light because its temperature is high.

D) The phenomenon occurs because the refractive index of air is zero near the road.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:**

A mirage is an atmospheric optical phenomenon caused by a temperature-dependent refractive-index gradient. Rays from the sky can curve through the layers, and under suitable conditions the ray path can involve total internal reflection. The eye traces the arriving rays backwards, producing an apparent image that resembles a water surface.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why an object seen through a plane glass window appears nearly in its true direction
question: The window has parallel faces, and the ray emerges into air on the opposite side. An object is viewed through a thin, parallel-sided glass window. Why is the apparent direction of the emergent ray the same as the direction of the incident ray, even though the ray bends inside the glass?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="120" y="15" width="80" height="145" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M10 130 L120 105 L200 91 L306 66" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M10 130 L306 66" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><text x="126" y="32" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Glass window</text><text x="14" y="146" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Object</text><text x="238" y="56" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text></svg>

options.text: The refractive index of glass is identical to that of air.
The second surface cancels the first surface's refraction because both surfaces are parallel, although a lateral displacement may remain.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection twice, restoring its original direction.
The ray bends towards the normal at both surfaces by equal angles.

explanation: The ray bends towards the normal on entering glass and away from the normal on leaving it. Parallel interfaces and the same external medium restore the original emergent direction. The emergent ray may still be laterally displaced. Option D is incorrect because the ray bends in opposite angular senses at the two interfaces.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Correct use of a right-angled prism in a periscope
question: A right-angled prism redirects a ray through 90^° using total internal reflection. A periscope uses a right-angled isosceles prism with refractive index 1.5. A ray enters normally through a short face and strikes the hypotenuse at 45^°. Which statement explains why this arrangement can replace a plane mirror?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 30 L30 105 L105 105 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M30 30 L105 105 L180 30 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M5 67 L30 67 L66 103 L66 145" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M66 145 L60 135 M66 145 L72 135" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="14" y="20" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Incident light</text><text x="78" y="158" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Reflected ray</text><text x="128" y="52" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Prism</text></svg>

options.text: The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the hypotenuse and can be redirected through 90^° with very little loss at the reflecting surface.
The ray is refracted by 90^° because the prism's refractive index is 1.5.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the hypotenuse only if the refractive index is less than 1.
The ray is absorbed by the prism and re-emitted in a perpendicular direction.

explanation: The critical angle for glass–air is approximately 41.8^°. The internal incidence angle of 45^° exceeds this value, so total internal reflection occurs. The ray is reflected through 90^° in this geometry, making the prism useful in optical instruments.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Correct interpretation of a ray diagram for a transparent medium
question: The refracted ray makes a smaller angle with the normal than the incident ray. The ray diagram shows light entering medium Q from medium P and bending towards the normal. Which additional conclusion is valid, assuming the same frequency of light is maintained across the boundary?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 185" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 85 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" /><rect x="10" y="87" width="300" height="82" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M45 20 L160 85 L270 146" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M160 12 V170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.1" /><text x="17" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium P</text><text x="17" y="105" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium Q</text><text x="173" y="25" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="205" y="137" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Ray in Q</text></svg>

options.text: The speed of light increases in Q, and the wavelength increases.
The frequency increases in Q, while the speed remains constant.
The speed decreases in Q, and the wavelength decreases.
The speed decreases in Q, but the wavelength increases.

explanation:
Bending towards the normal indicates entry into the optically denser medium for the given light. Thus the refractive index increases, and


v=(c / n)


decreases. Frequency remains unchanged, so lambda=v/f also decreases. Option D incorrectly predicts an increase in wavelength.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Determining the refractive index from a ray diagram
question: The angles shown are measured from the normal at the plane interface. The figure shows a ray passing from air into a transparent medium. The angle of incidence is 60^° and the angle of refraction is 35^°. Which is the approximate refractive index of the medium relative to air?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 195" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="98" width="300" height="85" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M10 98 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M160 20 V182" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.1" /><path d="M48 26 L160 98 L196 180" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M48 26 L160 98" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="16" y="118" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Transparent medium</text><text x="105" y="49" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = 60°</text><text x="166" y="126" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">r = 35°</text><text x="170" y="30" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text></svg>
explanation:
Using Snell's law,


n=(sin i / sin r)
=(sin60^° / sin35^°)



n=(0.8660 / 0.5736)≈1.51


The calculated value is approximately 1.51, so none of the listed options is correct as originally framed. To preserve accuracy, the question must be corrected.

**Corrected option D:** 1.51.

The other options are distractors arising from incorrect ratios or inaccurate trigonometric values.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Predicting whether a ray can emerge from a denser medium
question: A ray inside glass strikes the glass–air interface at 50^°. A ray travels inside glass of refractive index 1.5 and strikes a glass–air interface at 50^°. Which statement correctly predicts the ray path?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="95" width="300" height="80" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M10 95 H310 M160 15 V175" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M35 145 L160 95 L240 34" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M35 145 L160 95" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="17" y="114" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Glass (n = 1.5)</text><text x="17" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="174" y="26" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="74" y="132" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = 50°</text></svg>

options.text: It emerges into air at approximately 50^°.
It undergoes total internal reflection because 50^° exceeds the critical angle of approximately 41.8^°.
It emerges into air at 90^° because every ray travelling from glass to air grazes the surface.
It undergoes total internal reflection because the angle of refraction is 50^°.

explanation:
The critical angle is


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 1.5)right)
≈41.8^°


Since 50^°>C, total internal reflection occurs. Option C confuses the critical-angle condition with incidence above the critical angle.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Distinguishing a real image from an apparent image
question: The backward extensions of refracted rays appear to meet above the real object. A submerged object is viewed from air. The backward extensions of the refracted rays meet at a point above the object. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 195" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="78" width="300" height="105" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.18" /><path d="M10 78 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><circle cx="105" cy="150" r="5" fill="#D97706" /><circle cx="105" cy="127" r="4" fill="#0D9488" /><path d="M105 150 L160 78 L235 20" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M105 150 L235 20" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none" /><circle cx="235" cy="20" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><text x="18" y="23" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="18" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="114" y="123" font-size="10" fill="#0D9488">Apparent image</text><text x="114" y="165" font-size="10" fill="#D97706">Object</text><text x="242" y="22" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Eye</text></svg>

options.text: A real image forms in water because the refracted rays physically converge at that point.
The apparent image is virtual and cannot be located by ray tracing.
The apparent image is virtual because the refracted rays diverge towards the observer, while their backward extensions meet at the apparent position.
The apparent image is real because it is closer to the water surface.

explanation: A virtual image is formed where the backward extensions of rays appear to meet. The actual refracted rays do not physically converge there, so the image cannot be projected onto a screen at that apparent position. Option A confuses geometrical extensions with actual ray paths.

Which candidate correctly represents the refracted ray if the incident angle is 50^° and the refractive index of glass is 1.5?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
      <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Refraction Through Glass Slab: Lateral Displacement</text>
      <!-- Glass slab -->
      <rect x="100" y="65" width="260" height="70" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.8"/>
      <text x="330" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0369a1">Glass (Dense)</text>
      <!-- Incident Ray -->
      <line x1="60" y1="25" x2="160" y2="65" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Refracted Ray inside slab (bends towards normal) -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="220" y2="135" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Emergent Ray (parallel to incident) -->
      <line x1="220" y1="135" x2="320" y2="175" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Dotted original path -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="380" y2="153" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
      <!-- Lateral displacement line -->
      <line x1="270" y1="155" x2="285" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="310" y="140" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Lateral Displacement (d)</text>
      <text x="230" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Angle of Incidence i = Angle of Emergence e; Emergent ray is parallel to incident ray</text>
    </svg>

options.text: A ray in glass making an angle of approximately 75^° with the normal.
A ray in glass making an angle of approximately 30.7^° with the normal.
A ray in glass making an angle of 50^° with the normal.
A ray in glass making an angle of approximately 59.3^° with the normal.

explanation:
By Snell’s law,


n=(sin i / sin r)


Taking the refractive index of air as 1,


sin r=(sin50^° / 1.5)
=(0.7660 / 1.5)=0.5107


Therefore,


r≈30.7^°


The ray bends towards the normal on entering the optically denser glass. Option C ignores refraction, while A and D incorrectly predict bending away from the normal.

question: The incident ray is in glass; the refracted ray is in air. A ray travels from glass into air. The angle of incidence is 30^°, and the angle of refraction is 48.6^°. Which expression gives the refractive index of glass relative to air?

<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">

options.text: dfrac{sin48.6^°}{sin30^°}
dfrac{sin30^°}{sin48.6^°}
dfrac{sin30^°}{sin48.6^°}, interpreted as the absolute refractive index of air.
dfrac{sin48.6^°}{sin30^°}, interpreted as the refractive index of air relative to glass.

explanation:
For light travelling from glass to air,


n_{glass relative to air}
=(sin r / sin i)


Thus,


n=(sin48.6^° / sin30^°)
≈(0.75 / 0.5)=1.5


The ratio is reversed compared with the usual air-to-glass form of Snell’s law because the incident medium is now glass. Option B gives the reciprocal, approximately 0.67, which represents air relative to glass.

question: The slab faces are parallel; the incident and emergent rays lie on opposite sides of the slab. A ray enters a parallel-sided glass slab obliquely. Which statement correctly describes the emergent ray and the lateral displacement?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">

      <!-- Lateral displacement line -->
      <line x1="270" y1="155" x2="285" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="310" y="140" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Lateral Displacement (d)</text>
      <text x="230" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Angle of Incidence i = Angle of Emergence e; Emergent ray is parallel to incident ray</text>
    </svg>

options.text: The emergent ray bends towards the normal and has a different direction from the incident ray.
The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, but lateral displacement is always zero.
The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, and the lateral displacement increases if the slab thickness increases while the angle of incidence and refractive index remain fixed.
The emergent ray is perpendicular to the incident ray because the slab has two refracting surfaces.

explanation:
At the first surface, the ray bends towards the normal; at the second, it bends away from the normal. Because the two surfaces are parallel, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.

For a slab of thickness t,


d=t(sin(i-r) / cos r)


For fixed i and r, lateral displacement d is proportional to t. Option B is a tempting error: parallel rays need not coincide, and oblique incidence generally produces a non-zero lateral displacement.

options.text: Apparent depth 16 cm; apparent shift 4 cm downwards.
Apparent depth 9 cm; apparent shift 3 cm upwards.
Apparent depth 9 cm; apparent shift 3 cm downwards.
Apparent depth 12 cm; apparent shift zero.

explanation:
For near-normal viewing from air into water,


n=(real depth / apparent depth)


Hence,


apparent depth=(12 / 4/3)=9 cm


The apparent shift is


12-9=3 cm


The coin appears raised towards the surface. Option A results from inverting the depth ratio.

options.text: The angle of refraction is 90^°, and the angle of incidence is also 90^°.
The angle of incidence is 90^°, and the angle of refraction is the critical angle.
The angle of refraction is 0^°, and the angle of incidence is the critical angle.
The angle of refraction is 90^°, and the angle of incidence is the critical angle, approximately 41.8^°.

At the critical angle C, the refracted ray travels along the interface, so its angle with the normal is 90^°.


sin C=(1 / 1.5)=frac23

Option A confuses the grazing refracted ray’s angle with the incident angle. The critical angle is measured inside the denser medium.

title: Distinguishing critical refraction from total internal reflection
question: Ray at a denser-to-rarer boundary The incident ray is in glass; the refracted ray runs along the interface. A second ray is incident on the same glass–air boundary at 45^°. Which conclusion follows from the figure and the refractive index of glass?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="94" width="296" height="84" fill="#72B7E8" fill-opacity="0.25" /><path d="M12 94 H308" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M160 24 V170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M86 157 L160 94 L285 94" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M150 102 L160 94 L147 93" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="113" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Glass (n = 1.5)</text><text x="18" y="23" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air (n = 1)</text><text x="173" y="83" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">r = 90°</text><text x="120" y="140" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">C</text><circle cx="160" cy="94" r="3" fill="#D97706" /></svg>

options.text: The second ray refracts into air at 45^° because the angle is greater than the critical angle.
The second ray undergoes total internal reflection because its angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
The second ray refracts into air at 90^° because every angle greater than the critical angle produces grazing refraction.
The second ray passes undeviated into air because glass and air have the same boundary normal.

explanation:
The critical angle is


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 1.5)right)
≈41.8^°


Since 45^°>41.8^°, the ray undergoes total internal reflection. At exactly the critical angle, the refracted ray grazes the interface; above it, no ordinary refracted ray enters the air.

title: Testing both conditions for total internal reflection
question: Compare the two possible directions of incidence at the interface. Which of the following situations can produce total internal reflection?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="8" y="88" width="304" height="82" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M8 88 H312" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M160 18 V165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><path d="M58 147 L160 88 L246 28" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M160 88 L256 148" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 3" /><text x="15" y="108" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="15" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="167" y="72" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="179" y="115" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Possible ray</text></svg>

options.text: Light travels from air into water at 60^°.
Light travels from water into air at an incidence angle of 30^°, when the critical angle is approximately 49^°.
Light travels from glass into water at an angle greater than the critical angle for the glass–water pair.
Light travels from air into glass at an angle of 80^°.

explanation:
Total internal reflection requires both:

1. Light must travel from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium.
2. The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle for that pair of media.

Only C satisfies both conditions. A and D involve light entering a denser medium, while B has an incidence angle smaller than the critical angle.

question: The prism is a right-angled isosceles prism; internal incidence on the hypotenuse is 45^°. A ray enters one of the shorter faces of a right-angled isosceles glass prism normally. The refractive index of glass is 1.5. At the hypotenuse, the angle of incidence is 45^°. What happens?

The ray emerges through the hypotenuse because every prism face permits refraction.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection only if its angle of incidence is 90^°.
The ray bends towards the normal at the hypotenuse and enters air.

explanation: The critical angle for glass–air is approximately 41.8^°. Since 45^°>41.8^°, total internal reflection occurs at the hypotenuse. The ray is reflected internally, changing its direction by 90^°. Option B ignores the critical-angle condition.

title: Optical fibre: identifying the role of the core
question: The light ray repeatedly reflects at the core–cladding interface. An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.50 and cladding of refractive index 1.40. Which statement best explains the ray path shown?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="38" width="290" height="84" rx="4" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><rect x="15" y="53" width="290" height="54" rx="2" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M24 80 L75 56 L126 104 L177 56 L228 104 L285 76" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M277 70 L285 76 L275 80" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" /><text x="23" y="29" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Cladding (lower n)</text><text x="24" y="96" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Core (higher n)</text></svg>

options.text: The ray is guided because the core absorbs all the refracted light and re-emits it.
The ray is guided by total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface when the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle for that interface.
The ray is guided because the cladding has a higher refractive index than the core.
The ray is guided because the frequency of light increases at every reflection.

explanation:
The core has the higher refractive index, so light can undergo total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface.


sin C=(1.40 / 1.50)


Thus C≈69^°. For incidence angles inside the core greater than this critical angle, the ray remains guided. Option C reverses the refractive-index relationship.

question: The ray undergoes repeated internal reflections before emerging through a suitable face. A diamond has a very high refractive index, approximately 2.42. Which interpretation of the figure is correct?

options.text: The diamond sparkles because light travels faster inside it than in air.
The diamond sparkles because the frequency of light increases at each internal reflection.
The diamond sparkles because every incident ray undergoes total internal reflection, regardless of its angle.
The diamond can sparkle because its small critical angle allows many rays to undergo repeated total internal reflection before emerging.

explanation:
For diamond–air,


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 2.42)right)
≈24.4^°


This small critical angle makes total internal reflection possible for many internal rays. Suitable facets then direct light towards the observer. Option C is incorrect because rays incident at angles below the critical angle may refract out instead.

question: Starlight or sunlight bends progressively through atmospheric layers of varying refractive index. The Sun is geometrically just below the horizon, but the observer can still see its apparent image. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight progressively towards regions of higher refractive index, making the Sun appear higher than its geometric position.
The atmosphere reflects all sunlight at the horizon by total internal reflection.
The Sun appears higher because the speed of light increases continuously as it enters denser atmospheric layers.
Atmospheric refraction changes the frequency of sunlight until it becomes visible above the horizon.

explanation:
is correct?

A) Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight progressively towards regions of higher refractive index, making the Sun appear higher than its geometric position.

B) The atmosphere reflects all sunlight at the horizon by total internal reflection.

C) The Sun appears higher because the speed of light increases continuously as it enters denser atmospheric layers.

D) Atmospheric refraction changes the frequency of sunlight until it becomes visible above the horizon.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:**

Atmospheric density and refractive index generally increase closer to Earth's surface. Light curves through the atmosphere, and the backward extension of the final ray places the apparent Sun above its true geometric position. This causes advanced sunrise and delayed sunset. Option B incorrectly attributes the effect to total internal reflection.

Stars are point-like sources as seen from Earth, so changing atmospheric refraction causes noticeable fluctuations in their apparent brightness and position; planets have a measurable apparent disc that averages out many fluctuations.
Planets do not undergo atmospheric refraction because they are closer to Earth.
Stars twinkle because their light always undergoes total internal reflection in the atmosphere.

explanation: Turbulent atmospheric layers continuously change the refractive path of starlight. A star's tiny apparent angular size makes these fluctuations noticeable. A planet's apparent disc averages the effects over many rays, so its twinkling is usually less noticeable. Option C is false because planetary light also undergoes atmospheric refraction.

Every ray striking the bubble must refract into the air, regardless of its angle.
Light is produced inside the bubble by the compression of air.
Some incident rays in water undergo total internal reflection at the water–air boundary because water is optically denser than air.

explanation:
is physically consistent with the water–air interface?

A) The bubble is bright because its refractive index is higher than that of water.

B) Every ray striking the bubble must refract into the air, regardless of its angle.

C) Light is produced inside the bubble by the compression of air.

D) Some incident rays in water undergo total internal reflection at the water–air boundary because water is optically denser than air.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:**

The refractive index of water is higher than that of air. Rays travelling in water can undergo total internal reflection at the bubble boundary when their incidence angle exceeds the water–air critical angle. The reflected rays can make the bubble appear bright. Not every ray is necessarily totally internally reflected.

The test tube appears bright because all light entering the tube is absorbed and converted into visible light.

explanation:
?

A) The test tube appears bright because glass has a refractive index lower than both air and water.

B) The test tube appears bright because all light entering the tube is absorbed and converted into visible light.

C) Reflections, including possible total internal reflection at suitable denser-to-rarer interfaces, can direct light towards the observer; the effect depends on the ray angles and refractive indices.

The reciprocal of the refractive index of glass relative to air.
The speed of light in glass divided by the speed of light in air.
The critical angle of glass in degrees.

n=(sin i / sin r)


The gradient of a graph of sin i against sin r is


(Δ(sin i) / Δ(sin r))=n=1.5

n=(1 / sin C)

n_X=(1 / sin30^°)=2

For fixed i and r, lateral displacement d is proportional to t. Option B is a tempting error: parallel rays need not coincide, and oblique incidence generally produces a non-zero lateral displacement.
